newsitem.title: UK: Stress and woes cloud Britons' holidays -- survey.
newsitem.headline: Stress and woes cloud Britons' holidays -- survey.

text.p: Theft, health problems and rows with partners are some of the reasons Britons find going on holiday much more stressful than staying at home, according to a survey published on Monday.
While serious problems are rarely encountered, a large number of British holidaymakers spend their trip fretting things will go wrong.
And the survey, published by Barclaycard, found that out of 2,000 questioned, over 40 percent actually looked forward to going home at the end of their holiday.
Around 13.5 million Britons are expected to take an overseas holiday this year.

However, even a dream vacation can be clouded by holiday blues stemming from worries over money and illness, with a quarter of respondents saying they had been struck down by bad health and nearly a third saying they feared running out of money.
Couples, released from busy careers at home and thrown together for two weeks, are prone to bickering, with 42 percent of those questioned admitting to arguments.
"Holidays often put a strain on relationships as well as budgets and bring out the worst in people, especially if the holiday does not come up to expectations," said psychologist Trevor Jellis.
Jellis said the stress rating of going on holiday came somewhere between moving home and committing a minor violation of the law.
Despite the availability of insurance packages, health worries and fear of accidents feature high in the list.

Stomach upsets, food poisoning, accidents and serious diseases are a cause for concern - particularly as more and more travellers seek adventure in the less developed parts of Asia, South America and Africa.
Caribbean resorts are increasingly popular with rain-weary Britons, but are also high on the list of stressful destinations as people worry more and more about the risk of skin-cancer from the sun.
Most reported crime consists of petty theft or card fraud, with France, Spain and the United States listed by Barclaycard as the worst blackspots.
And tourists are not always on the right side of the law themselves.
Barclaycard found British tourists frequently broke foreign laws through driving offences, being drunk and disorderly or taking photographs in a restricted area. --London newsroom +44 171 542 7950
